steps: The four whorls of a flower, from the outside to the centre, are calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium.
Calyx is made up of sepals, which protect the flower in the bud stage.
Corolla is made up of petals, which are often coloured and attract pollinators.
Androecium is the male reproductive whorl and is made up of stamens.
Each stamen consists of a filament and an anther; the anther produces pollen grains.
Gynoecium is the female reproductive whorl and is made up of one or more carpels (pistils).
Each carpel consists of a stigma, style and ovary; the ovary contains ovules.
items.finalAnswer: A flower has four whorls: calyx (sepals), corolla (petals), androecium (stamens with filament and anther) and gynoecium (carpels with stigma, style and ovary containing ovules).

steps: Inside the ovule, a diploid megaspore mother cell undergoes meiosis and forms four haploid megaspores.
Three megaspores degenerate, while the remaining functional megaspore develops into the embryo sac.
The nucleus of the functional megaspore divides mitotically three times, producing eight haploid nuclei.
Three nuclei move to the micropylar end; one forms the egg cell and the other two form the synergids.
Three nuclei move to the opposite, chalazal end and form the antipodal cells.
The remaining two nuclei lie in the centre of the embryo sac and are called polar nuclei.
items.finalAnswer: One functional megaspore divides three times to form an eight-nucleate embryo sac; one nucleus forms the egg cell and two central nuclei form the polar nuclei.

steps: Stamen is the male reproductive part of a flower, whereas the carpel is the female reproductive part.
A stamen consists of a filament and anther; a carpel consists of stigma, style and ovary.
The anther produces pollen grains, whereas the ovary contains ovules.
The stigma receives pollen grains, and the style connects the stigma to the ovary.
items.finalAnswer: A stamen is the male flower part, made of a filament and anther that produces pollen; a carpel is the female flower part, made of stigma, style and ovary containing ovules.

items.figure: A labelled flower showing, from the outside towards the centre, sepals and petals, with the stamen (anther and filament) and carpel (stigma, style and ovary containing ovules).
steps: Write “petal” beside one of the broad parts surrounding the reproductive organs.
Write “sepal” beside one of the outer, leaf-like parts at the base of the flower.
Label the male part “stamen”; point to its pollen-bearing tip as “anther” and its stalk as “filament”.
Label the female part “carpel” or “pistil”; point to its top as “stigma”, its narrow middle as “style” and its swollen base as “ovary”.
If the ovary is shown cut open, label the structures inside it “ovules”.
items.finalAnswer: Label the flower: sepal, petal, anther, filament, stigma, style, ovary and ovules.

steps: Vegetative propagation is a type of asexual reproduction in which new plants develop from vegetative parts of the parent plant, such as stems, roots or leaves.
Modified stems can produce new plants. Examples include the eyes of a potato tuber, the bulb of an onion and the rhizome of ginger.
Modified roots can produce new plants. Examples include the tuberous roots of sweet potato and Dahlia.
Some leaves produce buds that grow into new plants; for example, buds along the leaf margins of Bryophyllum develop into plantlets.
Thus, modified stems, roots and leaves differ in the vegetative part that forms the new plant.
items.finalAnswer: Vegetative propagation produces new plants from parent plant parts: modified stems (potato, onion, ginger), roots (sweet potato, Dahlia) and leaves (Bryophyllum).

steps: Humans can use vegetative propagation to produce new plants from parts of a parent plant.
In cutting, a piece of stem, root or leaf is cut from the parent plant and planted in moist soil; it develops roots and shoots and grows into a new plant.
In layering, a low branch is bent down and covered with soil while it is still attached to the parent plant; after roots form, it is cut from the parent and planted separately.
In grafting, a shoot or bud (scion) from a desired plant is joined to the rooted stem (stock) of another plant; the joined parts grow together as one plant.
In tissue culture, a small piece of plant tissue is grown in a sterile nutrient medium; it forms many plantlets that can be transferred to soil.
items.finalAnswer: New plants can be raised from parent vegetative parts by cutting, layering, grafting and tissue culture.

steps: The sporophyte is the diploid (2n) generation of a plant; it develops from the zygote.
The sporophyte produces haploid (n) spores by meiosis.
The gametophyte is the haploid (n) generation; it develops from a spore.
The gametophyte produces gametes by mitosis.
After fertilisation, the male and female gametes fuse to form a diploid zygote, which develops into the sporophyte.
items.finalAnswer: The diploid sporophyte develops from a zygote and makes haploid spores by meiosis; the haploid gametophyte develops from a spore and makes gametes by mitosis.

steps: The life cycle of a flowering plant alternates between a diploid sporophyte generation and haploid gametophyte generations.
The mature flowering plant is the diploid sporophyte. In its anthers, meiosis produces haploid microspores, which develop into pollen grains, the male gametophytes.
In the ovule, meiosis produces megaspores; usually one functional megaspore develops into the embryo sac, the female gametophyte.
After pollination, a pollen grain germinates on the stigma and forms a pollen tube that carries the male gametes towards the ovule.
During fertilisation, a male gamete fuses with the egg to form a diploid zygote. The zygote develops into an embryo; the ovule becomes a seed and the ovary becomes a fruit.
When the seed germinates, the embryo grows into a new diploid sporophyte, completing the alternation of generations.
items.finalAnswer: Flowering plants alternate between a diploid sporophyte, which produces spores by meiosis, and haploid male and female gametophytes, which produce gametes; fertilisation forms the zygote that develops into a new sporophyte.
